passage:
The summer I turned fifteen, Grandfather was building the Linnet in his shed at Merrow Point from the plans his father drew sixty years ago. He had raced in the harbor regatta every August of his life, but his hands had grown stiff, so he taught me the steam box, and I bent each plank while he measured it. Mrs. Vale had asked to buy the boat for her grandson to sail on her first visit to the shed.

In July Mr. Corran, who sold us the cedar, rowed across the harbor to look at the hull. He watched Grandfather try to hold a pencil, and then he made his offer: he would finish the Linnet in his yard in time for the regatta and charge only for the varnish. Grandfather said he would think it over, which in our family can mean anything.

One morning a week later the fourth plank split from end to end. Grandfather held his hands up to the light as if they belonged to someone else. “I marked that bevel wrong, Ada,” he said, and he spent the afternoon measuring every frame again, finding each one where the plans put it, while I stood by the steam box and said nothing.

That evening I opened my steam log. On the day I bent the fourth plank he had gone a fair distance up the coast to see Mrs. Vale, and I had pulled the plank out after forty minutes instead of an hour, wanting it on before he came home. I showed him the page. He read it twice. Then he said a repaired plank in a hurried hull would split again in the first heat of August, and that next summer the two of us would rebuild the Linnet properly. The regatta would have to manage without her.

Mrs. Vale found another boat for her grandson, and Grandfather says next summer the way other people say tomorrow. I watched him fumble the latch on the shed door that night, three tries before it caught, and in my room I counted the months to June, and then counted them again.

passage:
For thirty-two years Ezra Holm kept the light on Gannet Point, the low headland guarding the channel into Kelby. Off the point lie the breakers of Tarrow Shoal; Kelby's harbor lamp burned two miles farther up, and on clear nights both lights were visible from the gallery. In fog a bell was rung by hand for every vessel that passed inside the point, and his daughter Lise kept the logbook. Soon after midnight one November night in 1871, as fog moved in, the schooner Merrow struck the shoal and three of her crew drowned before dawn.

Captain Danby, who had come down the coast on a fair wind, said he had taken Gannet's light for Kelby's harbor lamp and asked that the harbor lamp be painted red. The schooner's owners pressed for a new lens, calling the old one weak and its beam too dim to carry. The pilots of Kelby sent the board a petition: the Merrow's pilot, a stranger, had steered too close to the point, and every pilot working the channel ought to hold a license.

The inquiry found that the shoal had shifted since the charts were made, and it urged a lightship beside Tarrow. Holm had rung the bell all night, and Lise's logbook marks each stroke until dawn. He spent the week after the hearing on the rocks, striking a borrowed church bell into a heavy surf while Lise walked the beach marking where each stroke was drowned out.

The board had little money to spend, and a lightship would have consumed most of it. Its chairman, Amos Reddick, said that a man who had stood thirteen winters on the point knew its weather better than any inquiry, and on the keeper's account of the night the board ordered a heavier bell.

It went up in 1872, low on the rock where Lise's marks showed a stroke carried farthest. In the eighteen years Holm kept the light after that, nothing larger than a rowboat touched Tarrow in fog, and the bell still hangs where he placed it, struck by machine at his old rate of one stroke a minute.
